justification: Both compared pages are the kind of result 'sorting algorithms' actually surfaces: GeeksforGeeks is a listicle/index page (categorizes algorithms, links out to per-algorithm articles, has a 'library implementations' section naming qsort/Arrays.sort/etc. but no code on the page itself, no stability treatment beyond a mention, no n log n lower bound); Programiz is a basic overview with a complexity/stability comparison table but no runnable code, no worked measurements, no lower-bound proof, and nothing about what any specific language's built-in sort actually does. (Real Python's sorting-algorithms page, a plausible third competitor, returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch and could not be read; its Python/Timsort focus would not directly compete with a C#-first article regardless.) Against both pages this article is clearly ahead, not just incrementally better: it implements and counts insertion, selection, merge, quicksort and heap sort with real machine-verified output rather than describing them; it proves the Ω(n log n) comparison-sort floor with a decision-tree diagram and then checks the floor against an exhaustive scan of all 40,320 permutations of 8 elements, not an assertion; it empirically demonstrates stability (and instability) for all five algorithms plus Array.Sort and OrderBy against the same ticket dataset, rather than a static stable/unstable table; and it ties every one of those results to what .NET's Array.Sort/List<T>.Sort/OrderBy actually run, citing both the documented introsort behavior and the current dotnet/runtime source (ArraySortHelper.cs, Array.cs) for the 16-element cutoff, the heapsort trigger and median-of-three pivoting. No other page checked does any of this. Sourcing is unusually solid for this pass: I fetched every primary source cited with a direct quotation (algs4 sections 2.1, 2.2, 2.3 and 2.4; the Array.Sort, List<T>.Sort and Enumerable.OrderBy docs; ArraySortHelper.cs and Array.cs) and every quoted fragment matches its source verbatim -- 'uses only a small auxiliary stack', the lightning-strike sentence, the standard-deviation sentence, the three Array.Sort algorithm-selection bullets, the IntrosortSizeThreshold '16 seems to speed up' comment, the median-of-three comment, the List<T>.Sort and OrderBy stability sentences, and the algs4 compare-count claims for all five algorithms. None of the multiple misquotes the writer says were self-corrected during drafting survived into this draft. All ten front-matter sources are cited inline at the point of the claim they support (unlike this pillar's own binary-search round 1, which lost points for exactly that gap), so the pilot-round 'cite where the claim is made' rule is met throughout, not just in the source list. No filler: the opening paragraph states a real, countable result (14 vs 7 vs 28 comparisons) instead of scene-setting, and the closing section is a decision table plus four questions that route a reader to a row, not a restated-headings summary. No keyword stuffing. Structure is not templated against its published siblings: compared with binary-search.md (a 'D' debugging-story shape opening on a buggy timetable lookup, six problem-driven headings, exercises named 'Trace it on paper first' / 'The loop that never returns' / 'Count a time window') and big-o-notation.md (a 'W' shape opening on a race-timing app, headings built around a single running argument), this article's 'C' comparison shape (one heading per algorithm, ending in a decision table), its different opening device (an array run through two algorithms side by side), and its exercise forms (predict-the-counts, find-the-bug, measure-it x2, extend-the-code, prove-it) do not reread as the same template with different nouns. I confirmed directly that it does not reuse big-o-notation.md's insertion-vs-merge-sort crossover demo: that demo times both sorts in nanoseconds across doubling sizes 8-2048 with an Optimize=true build flag to show where constants flip the winner; this article's insertion/selection sections instead count exact comparisons on a single fixed 8-element array with no timing at all, and the one place it touches the crossover result it does so by cross-reference ('as the earlier section on big-O's hidden constants measures directly') rather than by repeating the experiment -- a citation, not a duplicate. Five distinctive sentences web-searched in quotes returned no hits on any source other than the algs4/Microsoft Learn/GitHub pages already cited, so nothing reads as lifted from elsewhere uncredited. docs/crosslinks/algorithms/sorting-algorithms-compared.md exists and lists four sensible, specifically placed links to planned-but-unpublished siblings with stated boundaries, so the missing body links to best-average-worst-case and heaps-and-priority-queues are not a finding. I could not find a genuine policy-level defect to hold the score below 9.0; it is withheld from 10 only because I was unable to survey the full first page of live results for 'sorting algorithms' (WebSearch budget was exhausted this session) or read Real Python's competing page, so 'clearly better than the single best-ranking result' is not fully confirmed rather than confirmed-and-exceeded.
